title: Creation and Providence
subtitle: How and when God made the world, and how he holds it together now.
triageNote: That God made everything from nothing, that it was good, and that he sustains it, is first-order. All faithful Christians share it. The age of the earth and the mechanism of creation are matters where members of one faithful church can disagree without dividing.
question: When you confess that God made the heavens and the earth, you are saying something every Christian agrees on. But how did he do it, and when. Were the days of Genesis 1 ordinary twenty-four hour days, and is the earth a few thousand years old. Or is the earth billions of years old, with those days standing for long ages. Did God shape each creature directly, or did he work through the slow process that scientists call evolution. And is Genesis 1 even trying to answer those questions, or is it telling us something else entirely. This entry walks through four ways faithful Christians have answered, and tries to show each one at its strongest.
whyItMatters:
A new believer often arrives carrying a quiet fear. Somewhere they have been told that they must choose. Either you trust the Bible, or you use your mind. Either you believe Genesis, or you believe the people in lab coats. That choice is false. It has cost the church dearly.

Generations of young Christians have walked away from the faith, and not because the gospel failed them. Someone handed them an unnecessary either-or. They were taught that the whole structure stands or falls on the age of the earth. So when a geology class or a biology textbook made the young earth hard to hold, they thought the whole thing must be coming down. It was not the resurrection that broke. It was a fence someone had built too close to the road.

The church has long called the doctrine of creation out of nothing creation ex nihilo. God did not shape the world out of some pre-existing stuff. He called it into being where there had been nothing at all. That doctrine is the bedrock. So is the goodness of what he made. So is providence, the teaching that God did not wind the world up and walk away. He sustains and governs it every moment. Those are not up for debate here. What is up for debate is the how and the when. How we hold that question shapes whether we lose young believers needlessly or teach them that faith has room for honest thought.

positions.name: Young-earth creationism
positions.inOneLine: The days of Genesis 1 are ordinary days, the earth is thousands of years old, and the flood of Noah explains much of the rock and fossil record.
positions.bestCase:
I begin where the text begins. When Moses writes that there was evening and there was morning, the first day, and then the second, and so on through six, he is using the plain Hebrew word for day, yom. It is attached to a number and bracketed by evening and morning. Everywhere else in the Old Testament that this construction appears it means an ordinary day. I am not forcing a modern science onto the text. I am refusing to bend the text to fit a science that keeps changing.

This is what young-earth creationism holds, that God made the world in six ordinary days a few thousand years ago. The genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11, which count the years from Adam forward, give us a real and short timeline. I take those genealogies as history because the New Testament does. When Luke traces Jesus back to Adam, he is not telling a parable.

I also take the flood seriously as a global event. A worldwide flood that buried billions of creatures under fast-moving water and sediment would lay down exactly the kind of layered rock and fossil record we find. Much of what is read as millions of years of slow deposit is better read as the violent work of one catastrophic year. The earth looks old in places because something enormous happened to it, not because it is old.

And I worry about what we lose when we let the long ages in. If there were millions of years before Adam, then there were animals living and dying and being torn apart long before any human sinned. But Scripture ties death to sin. Paul says death came through one man. I would rather hold a young earth and keep death as the intruder it is than gain deep time and lose the goodness of the original world.

I know I am told this puts me at odds with most scientists. I have made peace with that. The same Word that was trustworthy to the martyrs is trustworthy to me, and I will read it as it presents itself before I read it through the lens of the latest journal.

positions.name: Old-earth creationism
positions.inOneLine: The earth is billions of years old, the days of Genesis 1 are long ages or a frame for stages, and God created across deep time without using common descent.
positions.bestCase:
I hold what is called old-earth creationism, and within it I am drawn to two related readings. The first is the day-age view, which takes the word day in Genesis 1 to mean a long age rather than twenty-four hours. The Hebrew word yom can mean an era, as it does when Scripture speaks of the day of the Lord. That day is plainly not a single sunrise. The second is progressive creation, which says God acted directly and repeatedly across that long span. He brought new kinds of life into being in stages rather than letting one creature descend from another.

I did not arrive here by caving to science, though I do take the rocks and the stars seriously. The light from distant galaxies, the rates at which certain elements decay, the thickness of ice and sediment laid down one quiet year at a time. All of these point the same direction, toward an earth of great age. I believe God does not lie in his world any more than he lies in his Word. Both are his.

This approach is sometimes called concordism. It is the conviction that the Bible and the findings of science, when each is read rightly, agree rather than collide. I find that older and wiser heads went before me here. Benjamin Warfield, who defended the full truth of Scripture as fiercely as anyone, allowed for an ancient earth. So did Charles Hodge. These were not men soft on the Bible. They simply did not think Genesis required a young earth.

Notice what I keep. I keep God as the direct cause of each major step. I keep Adam as a real man. I keep creation out of nothing. I do not need the slow chain of common descent to explain the diversity of life, because I believe God acted again and again across the ages. So I gain the deep time the world seems to show without giving up the direct hand of God that Scripture proclaims.

What I ask of my young-earth brother is only this. Let the word day carry the range it carries elsewhere in the Bible, and let the world God made testify alongside the Word he spoke.

positions.name: Evolutionary creation
positions.inOneLine: God created through the long process of evolution, so common descent and the truth of Genesis are not at war.
positions.bestCase:
I am a Christian and I am also persuaded by the science of common descent, the finding that all living things share ancestry and that life unfolded over billions of years through the process called evolution. The older name for my view is theistic evolution. Many of us now prefer evolutionary creation, because the noun is creation and the adjective is the method. God is the Creator. Evolution is how he did it.

I did not give up my Bible to get here. I gave up a particular reading of it. When I look closely at Genesis 1 and 2, I see two accounts that differ in order. In chapter one, plants come before man. In chapter two, the man is formed and then the garden is planted. If the writer had wanted a literal lab report, he would not have left that tension on the page. He was after something deeper than sequence.

John Walton has helped me see that the people who first received Genesis would have read it as an account of God assigning roles and taking up his rest in the cosmos as in a temple. It was not a timeline of material manufacture. Read that way, the chapter is not even trying to compete with biology. It is telling me whose world this is and why it exists.

Francis Collins led the effort to map the human genome and came to Christ as an adult. He has shown me that the DNA we carry tells the same story the fossils tell. I do not think God planted false evidence in my cells. I think he wove the long story of life and then, at a point of his choosing, breathed his own image into the creature he had prepared. Denis Alexander has written carefully about how Adam can be understood within this.

So I refuse the war. I will not tell a bright young believer in a biology class that she must choose between her Savior and the evidence in front of her. I will tell her that the God who raised Jesus is also the God who patiently grew a world. She may keep both.

positions.name: The framework view
positions.inOneLine: Genesis 1 is arranged by theme rather than by clock, so it makes no claim at all about the age of the earth.
positions.bestCase:
I hold what is called the framework hypothesis, sometimes called the literary framework view. My claim is simple. Genesis 1 is structured like a poem with a pattern. The pattern, not a calendar, is the point. Once you see the pattern, the question of how long it took stops being a question the text is asking.

Look at the six days as two columns of three. On days one to three God forms the empty places. Light, then sky and sea, then dry land. On days four to six God fills those same places in the same order. The lights of day four fill the light of day one. The birds and fish of day five fill the sky and sea of day two. The animals and man of day six fill the dry land of day three. The forming days are matched by the filling days. That is craftsmanship, not chronology.

This is why I say the framework view makes no claim about the age of the earth. I am not arguing for a young earth or an old earth. I am saying that Genesis 1 was never measuring the earth's age, so I will not press it to deliver a number it never promised. Meredith Kline and Henri Blocher have laid this out with care, and I find it both reverent toward the text and free of the fights that divide my friends.

Notice also the seventh day. The first six days each close with evening and morning. The seventh has no such ending. The rest of God is presented as ongoing. That alone suggests the days are doing something other than ticking off ordinary sunrises. They are a literary house in which the truth of God as Maker is furnished room by room.

What I gain is peace. I do not have to defend the age of the earth from this chapter, because this chapter is not making a case about it. I can let the geologists do geology and let Genesis do what it came to do, which is to tell me that the one true God made it all, made it good, and made it for his glory.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The opening chapter narrates six days of creative work, each closing with the refrain that there was evening and morning, followed by a seventh day of rest. It is the central battleground of the whole question.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hardest for the views that do not take the days as ordinary, because the plain refrain of evening and morning sounds like ordinary days.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The young-earth reader takes the days as twenty-four hours each. The old-earth reader takes day to mean a long age, as the word can elsewhere. The evolutionary-creation reader takes the chapter as an account of God ordering and assigning purpose rather than a timeline. The framework reader takes the six days as a thematic pattern of forming and filling, not a sequence of calendar dates.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Evolutionary creation and the framework view.
biblicalEvidence.summary: A second account of creation centered on the garden, the forming of Adam from the dust, and the making of Eve. Its order of events differs from chapter one, with the man formed before the plants of the garden are grown.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hardest for strict literal readings that expect a single unbroken chronological sequence, because chapter two does not line up step for step with chapter one.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Evolutionary-creation and framework readers point to the difference in order as a sign that Genesis 1 was never meant as a literal sequence. Young-earth and old-earth readers treat chapter two as a closer, complementary look at day six rather than a competing timeline, with the order being topical rather than strictly chronological.

biblicalEvidence.summary: In giving the Sabbath command, God grounds the seven-day week in his own pattern. In six days the Lord made heaven and earth and rested on the seventh, so Israel works six days and rests on the seventh.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hardest for the old-earth and evolutionary views, because the human work week is patterned on God's creative days, which seems to put the two on the same scale.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The young-earth reader sees this as confirmation that the days were ordinary, since our ordinary week mirrors them. Old-earth and framework readers respond that an analogy does not require the two sides to be the same length. The pattern of six-then-one can hold whether the original days were hours or ages or a literary frame. A son can imitate his father's rhythm of work without matching his father's size.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Old-earth and framework readings, and providence generally.
biblicalEvidence.summary: A long hymn praising God as the one who laid the earth's foundations, set the waters in place, feeds every creature, and renews the face of the ground. It follows roughly the order of Genesis 1 but as praise, not chronology.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hardest for any view that treats the Genesis order as a rigid scientific sequence, because here the same material is handled freely as worship.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Framework and old-earth readers note that this psalm takes the creation account and sings it, suggesting the original was always more than a bare timeline. Young-earth readers receive it as praise that assumes the literal account underneath. All four read it as a clear witness to providence, since the psalm dwells on God feeding and sustaining his creatures moment by moment.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Young-earth and old-earth creationism, on the historical Adam.
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul argues that sin and death entered the world through one man, Adam, and that salvation comes through one man, Christ. The logic sets Adam and Christ in parallel as two real heads of humanity.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hardest for any view that treats Adam as merely symbolic, because Paul's whole argument leans on Adam being as real as Christ. It also presses the young-earth concern about death before the fall.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Young-earth and old-earth readers take this as strong evidence for the historical Adam, a real first man whose fall brought death. Evolutionary-creation readers who hold this passage seriously argue that God could have chosen a real pair from among early humanity to bear his image and stand as covenant head. Adam is then historical without requiring that no creature existed before him. The debate over whether the death Paul means is human spiritual death or all biological death shapes the disagreement over animal death.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The Word who is God was in the beginning, and all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that has been made. Creation is the work of the eternal Son.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is not hard for any of the four views. It cuts against only the idea that the world made itself or arose from no maker at all.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All four read this together. It establishes that whatever the how and the when, the who is the eternal Word, and the from-what is nothing at all. This is the creation out of nothing that none of the four positions questions.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared by all four, and central to providence.
biblicalEvidence.summary: By Christ all things were created, in heaven and on earth, and in him all things hold together. He is before all things and the one in whom the universe coheres.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is not hard for any of the four. It presses only against deism, the idea of a God who creates and then withdraws.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All four hold this as common ground. The phrase that in him all things hold together is one of the clearest statements of providence in Scripture. The world does not run on its own. It is upheld by Christ in every instant. None of the four disputes this.

weighing:
Here is my own judgment, offered as a judgment and not as a test of fellowship, because this question is genuinely third-order. I find the framework view the most careful reading of Genesis 1 as a piece of writing. The pattern of forming and filling is really there on the page, and the seventh day really does lack the closing refrain. That pattern persuades me. The chapter was not built to be a clock. If that is right, then much of the fight over twenty-four hours versus long ages is a fight over a question the text is not asking.

On the science of the age of the earth, I lean toward the old-earth conviction that the world is ancient. The evidence in rock and light seems to me to point that way with one voice. And I do not believe God would write one story in his world and a contradicting one in his Word. I hold that lightly. I have real respect for young-earth brothers and sisters who have thought hard and concluded otherwise. They are guarding something precious, the trustworthiness of the plain sense of Scripture, and I would rather stand near someone who guards that too closely than near someone who does not guard it at all.

The one place I grow more cautious is the historical Adam. I am persuaded that the New Testament needs a real Adam for Paul's argument in Romans to hold, and so I treat that as weightier than the age of the earth, though even there faithful people differ on the details. The mechanism, whether God shaped each kind directly or worked through common descent, I leave more open than I leave Adam.

So my settled feeling is this. Be relaxed about the days and the years. Be careful about Adam. Be certain about the maker, the goodness, and the sustaining hand. And hold the rest with an open palm.
charitableDisagreement:
If you are new to the faith and you have read this far, hear the main thing plainly. You can love Jesus with your whole heart and hold any of these four views. The young-earth grandmother and the old-earth physics teacher and the framework pastor can take communion at the same rail and mean every word of the creed together. They agree on everything the creed actually says. God made the heavens and the earth. He made it out of nothing. He made it good. He holds it together still.

What divides them is a set of honest questions about how and when, and those questions, real as they are, do not touch the gospel. Study them. Argue them with warmth and with books open. But do not let anyone tell you that your salvation, or anyone else's, rides on the age of a rock. This is not a hill to die on.

relatedDebates.note: Whether Adam was a real first man or a symbol of early humanity matters more than the age of the earth, because Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 sets Adam in parallel with Christ. If the parallel is to hold, Adam needs to be as historical as Christ. The historical Adam, meaning an actual first human through whom sin entered, is held firmly by young-earth and old-earth readers and by many evolutionary-creation readers as well. They locate a real Adam within early humanity. A purely symbolic Adam strains the logic of the New Testament. The age of the earth never does that. This is why thoughtful people treat it as a heavier question.

If the earth is ancient, then animals were living and dying for ages before any human sinned. Young-earth readers see this as a serious cost, since Scripture ties death to sin and calls the original creation good. Old-earth and evolutionary readers answer that the death Paul speaks of is human death under judgment. Animal death within the original good world is a different thing, part of how a world of lions and lambs and seasons actually works. The two sides are really disagreeing about what kind of death the curse introduced.

Beyond the act of creation stands the ongoing work of providence, God sustaining and governing all things. Two terms help. Concurrence is the teaching that God and his creatures both truly act in the same event, so that when a farmer grows wheat, God genuinely gives the growth and the farmer genuinely works, without either canceling the other. The other hard edge is the problem of evil, the question of how a good and sovereign God governs a world that holds real suffering. Providence does not solve that pain. But it refuses to leave us with a God who has stepped away. The same Christ in whom all things hold together is the one who entered the suffering himself.
